power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Beyond the Battlefield: A Cross-Sectional Study of War-Related Stressors and Mental Health in Four Central European Countries

author.affiliation:
University of the National Education Commission
								
									Krakow
									Poland

text.text: Prolonged armed conflicts may affect mental health beyond the battlefield through indirect, war-related stressors.
However, evidence on populations outside the immediate conflict zone remains limited.

This study assessed psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and examined their associations with coping strategies among adults in four Central European countries more than two and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in October 2024 with 2,962 participants from Poland (n = 728), Czechia (n = 743), Slovakia (n = 742), and Hungary (n = 749).
Participants were recruited from opt-in online research panels using stratified quota sampling based on sociodemographic characteristics.

Psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms were measured using the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), the Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7), and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), respectively.
Betweencountry differences were examined using one-way analysis of variance, and associated factors were assessed using country-specific linear regression models.
Poland had the highest mean scores for psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (K10: F(3, 2,958) = 12.61; GAD-7: F(3, 2,958) = 9.40; PHQ-9: F(3, 2,958) = 7.10; all p < 0.001).
text.formatted: Poland had the highest mean scores for psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms (K10: F(3, 2,958) = 12.61; GAD-7: F(3, 2,958) = 9.40; PHQ-9: F(3, 2,958) = 7.10; all p < 0.001).

text.text: Czechia had the lowest mean scores for distress and anxiety.
Mean depressive symptom scores were lower in Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary than in Poland, with no significant differences among the three countries.
The average item-level selection rate was higher for problem-focused than for emotion-focused strategies in all four countries.
Younger age, lower perceived quality of life, and greater use of emotion-focused coping were associated with higher symptom scores.
Problem-focused coping was associated with lower symptom scores only in Poland.
Mental health symptom scores differed across the four countries, as did some associations between coping strategies and mental health.
The findings support continued monitoring and attention to groups reporting poorer outcomes.
Given the cross-sectional design, the observed associations do not establish causal effects.
Armed conflict can affect people beyond those directly exposed to combat through economic disruption, perceived threats, displacement, media coverage, and uncertainty [1] [2] [3].
text.formatted: Armed conflict can affect people beyond those directly exposed to combat through economic disruption, perceived threats, displacement, media coverage, and uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: In this article, we use "transboundary mental health consequences" to describe conflict-related mental health outcomes among populations outside combat zones whose lives are connected to the conflict through social, economic, political, or informational processes.

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 displaced millions of Ukrainians across Europe [4], raising public health concerns about access to healthcare and health needs in host countries [5].
text.formatted: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 displaced millions of Ukrainians across Europe <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, raising public health concerns about access to healthcare and health needs in host countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary share a border with Ukraine; Czechia does not, although it has hosted many Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection relative to its population [6].
text.formatted: Poland, Slovakia, and Hungary share a border with Ukraine; Czechia does not, although it has hosted many Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection relative to its population <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The four countries also differ in refugee reception and in their political and institutional contexts, making them a useful setting in which to examine how conflict-related concerns extend beyond areas of active fighting.
Across Central Europe, the invasion coincided with rising energy and food prices, inflation, supply-chain disruption, and financial uncertainty for households [7, 8].
text.formatted: Across Central Europe, the invasion coincided with rising energy and food prices, inflation, supply-chain disruption, and financial uncertainty for households <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: It also renewed concerns about military escalation, nuclear threats, security, military spending, refugee support, and the war's trajectory [9].
text.formatted: It also renewed concerns about military escalation, nuclear threats, security, military spending, refugee support, and the war's trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: Mental health may therefore be associated with several concurrent stressors.
The stress process framework helps explain how conflict-related stress may become relevant to everyday life.
Pearlin and colleagues describe how stressful experiences can generate secondary stressors across different life domains [10].
text.formatted: Pearlin and colleagues describe how stressful experiences can generate secondary stressors across different life domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: During a prolonged conflict, security concerns may coexist with worries about finances, family safety, public services, and political stability.

Conservation of resources theory offers a complementary perspective: threats to valued resources, including income, housing, health, social relationships, and personal control, may undermine psychological well-being [11].
text.formatted: Conservation of resources theory offers a complementary perspective: threats to valued resources, including income, housing, health, social relationships, and personal control, may undermine psychological well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Social support may provide emotional reassurance and practical assistance amid continuing uncertainty [12].
text.formatted: Social support may provide emotional reassurance and practical assistance amid continuing uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: The information environment may also shape perceptions of threat.
News and social media provide continuous reports about the conflict, civilian casualties, and possible escalation [13] [14] [15].
text.formatted: News and social media provide continuous reports about the conflict, civilian casualties, and possible escalation <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Since the full-scale invasion, research has documented distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe [16] [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: Since the full-scale invasion, research has documented distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms in Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: War-related concern and attention to conflict news have also been associated with poorer mental health [13, 17, 20].
text.formatted: War-related concern and attention to conflict news have also been associated with poorer mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20]</ref>.

text.text: Institutional trust may influence how people respond to uncertainty: confidence in security institutions and public authorities may strengthen perceptions of predictability and protection, while interpersonal trust and social support may shape how people experience and manage stress [21].
text.formatted: Institutional trust may influence how people respond to uncertainty: confidence in security institutions and public authorities may strengthen perceptions of predictability and protection, while interpersonal trust and social support may shape how people experience and manage stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: These relationships may vary with individual circumstances and the wider institutional and information context.
Coping strategies are another potential correlate of mental health.
Problem-focused coping involves efforts to address a stressor, solve problems, or seek advice and support.
Emotionfocused coping involves attempts to regulate emotional responses and may include distraction, minimisation, prayer, the use of sedatives or other substances, and resignation [22, 23].

text.text: This study compares survey respondents from Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary using data collected in October 2024.

It examines cross-country differences in psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and assesses factors associated with these outcomes in country-specific regression models, with particular attention to coping strategies.
The study addresses three research questions: RQ1: Do psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptom scores differ among survey respondents in Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary?
RQ2: Which demographic, socioeconomic, psychosocial, institutional, media-related, and war-related factors are associated with these outcomes in each country?
RQ3: How are problem-focused and emotion-focused coping strategies associated with psychological distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms in the country-specific models?

A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in October 2024, more than two and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
Data were collected concurrently in Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary by European National Panels (ENP), a research company specialising in online social research in Central and Eastern Europe.
The questionnaire was translated into the national language of each country and reviewed by researchers there for linguistic clarity and contextual appropriateness.
ENP's online panels comprised approximately 23,000 registered members in Poland, 64,000 in Czechia, 25,000 in Slovakia, and 24,000 in Hungary.
Stratified quota sampling was used to recruit participants and obtain variation by gender, age, place of residence, education, and financial situation.

Because participants were recruited from opt-in online panels rather than population registers, the samples should not be considered strictly probability-based or fully representative of the national populations.
Methodological research has compared the sociodemographic characteristics of online and offline populations and examined the effects of including offline respondents on survey estimates [25].

text.text: Following data-quality checks by ENP, the final sample comprised 2,962 respondents: 728 from Poland, 743 from Czechia, 742 from Slovakia, and 749 from Hungary.
Participation was voluntary and anonymous.
Before starting the questionnaire, respondents were informed about the study's purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality, and their right to withdraw.
Informed consent was obtained electronically.
The survey was conducted in accordance with the ESOMAR Code of Conduct.

text.text: The scale measures nonspecific symptoms of psychological distress experienced during the preceding four weeks.
Each item was rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (none of the time) to 5 (all of the time).
Responses were summed to produce a total score ranging from 10 to 50, with higher scores indicating greater psychological distress.

Respondents reported their gender, age, education, place of residence, marital status, and number of children.

Perceived personal financial consequences of the war were assessed by asking whether the war in Ukraine had serious financial consequences for respondents personally.

Perceived economic consequences for the country were assessed by asking whether the war had serious economic consequences for the respondent's country; the country name was adapted for each national sample.
Both items were originally rated on a five-point scale ranging from 1 (definitely yes) to 5 (definitely no).
Responses were reverse-coded so that higher scores indicated more severe perceived consequences (1 = definitely no,5 = definitely yes).
Perceived social support was assessed using two questions: how many people respondents could talk to about personal problems and how many they could rely on for help.
Responses ranged from 1 (no one) to 6 (more than ten people).
Responses of "difficult to say" were treated as missing.
The mean of the two items was calculated for respondents with valid responses to both.
Higher scores indicated greater available social support.
Internal consistency ranged from acceptable to good across the four countries (Cronbach's α: Poland = .798, Czechia = .765, Slovakia = .765, and Hungary = .835).
Quality of life was measured using the Cantril Self-Anchoring Striving Scale [30].
text.formatted: Quality of life was measured using the Cantril Self-Anchoring Striving Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Respondents rated their current life on a ladder ranging from 1 (the worst possible life) to 10 (the best possible life).
Higher scores indicated a more favourable assessment of quality of life.
Institutional trust was assessed in relation to 13 public and social institutions, each rated on a four-point scale ranging from 1 (definitely do not trust) to 4 (definitely trust).
Exploratory factor analyses were conducted separately in each country using principal axis factoring with oblimin rotation.
These analyses identified a recurring cluster of four items: trust in the armed forces, the police, the Border Guard, and local authorities.

The trust in security and local public institutions index was calculated as the mean of these four items for respondents with valid responses to at least three items; cases with fewer than three valid responses were treated as missing.
Higher scores indicated greater trust.
Sampling adequacy was good across countries (KMO = .850-.897), and Bartlett's tests of sphericity were significant in all four countries (all p < .001).

Interpersonal trust was assessed with a single question asking whether respondents trusted other people.
Response options were yes, no, and "I don't know".
For the regression analyses, responses were recoded into a binary indicator of lack of interpersonal trust:0 = trust (yes) and1 = distrust or indecision (no or "I don't know").
Trust served as the reference category.
Thus, positive regression coefficients indicate higher mental health symptom scores among respondents who reported distrust or were undecided than among those who reported trust.

Media use was assessed using seven items measuring how often respondents watched television on a television set, watched television online, listened to the radio, listened to podcasts, read printed newspapers, read online news, and used online social networking services.
Responses were recorded on a six-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 6 (daily or almost daily), with higher scores indicating more frequent use.
The items were grouped into three indicators.
Traditional media use was calculated as the mean frequency of watching television on a television set, listening to the radio, and reading printed newspapers.
Digital media use was calculated as the mean frequency of watching television online, listening to podcasts, and reading online news.
Social media use was measured using the single item on the frequency of using online social networking services.
Respondents were presented with a list of 16 potential threats that could negatively affect their lives and were asked to select the three they considered most important.

Three options were classified as military or nuclear threats: the possible spread of the war to the respondent's country, the use of nuclear weapons, and a nuclear accident at the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
A binary indicator of military and nuclear threat salience was coded 1 if a respondent selected at least one of these three options and 0 if none was selected.
The latter category served as the reference category.

Coping was measured using a checklist derived from the Polish Social Diagnosis study [31] and organised conceptually according to the distinction between problem-focused and emotionfocused coping [32].

text.text: Respondents indicated which strategies they used when facing difficult life situations.
Each strategy was coded 1 if selected and 0 if not selected; multiple responses were permitted.
Problem-focused coping comprised two strategies: seeking advice or assistance from other people and mobilising oneself to take protective action.
The problem-focused coping index was the number of these strategies selected and ranged from 0 to 2.

Emotion-focused coping comprised six strategies: using alcohol, cigarettes, or other substances; cognitively minimising the situation by thinking that things could be worse; taking sedatives; praying for help; engaging in distracting or mood-enhancing activities; and resignation or helplessness.
The emotion-focused coping index was the number of these strategies selected and ranged from 0 to 6.
The response "none of the above" was not included in either index.
Because these indices represent counts of heterogeneous coping responses rather than reflective psychometric scales, internal consistency was not used as the primary criterion for evaluating them.
Sample characteristics and the distributions of coping strategies were summarised separately for each country using frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations.
Betweencountry differences in mean K10, GAD-7, and PHQ-9 scores were examined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons.
Ordinary least-squares (OLS) linear regression models were estimated separately for Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary.

text.text: This study examined mental health symptoms among respondents in four Central European countries and identified factors associated with those symptoms.
Symptom levels were generally highest in Poland and lowest in Czechia, although not all pairwise country comparisons were statistically significant.

This pattern is consistent with findings from an 11country study, which reported the poorest mental health among residents of Ukraine, followed by residents of countries bordering Ukraine, and lower symptom levels in countries farther from the conflict in Ukraine [22].

This is consistent with conservation of resources theory, which links access to resources with psychological well-being [40], but the cross-sectional data cannot determine the direction of this association or rule out other explanations.

text.text: The revised social-support index, calculated as the mean of two items and coded so that higher scores indicated greater support, was inversely associated with K10 distress in all four countries and with GAD-7 scores in Hungary.
For PHQ-9, the association was positive in Slovakia and negative in Hungary, indicating that its direction varied across countries.
The cross-sectional data cannot establish whether social support reduces symptoms or whether mental health influences perceived support.
Associations involving institutional and interpersonal trust varied by country and symptom outcome.
Higher institutional trust was associated with lower scores in some models, while interpersonal distrust or indecision was associated with higher scores in a smaller number of models.
Military or nuclear threat salience was not independently associated with any outcome in the adjusted models.
The findings relate primarily to the model's mental-health domain and its proposed links with individual resources, social attitudes, and institutional trust.
Because societal resilience and public policy preparedness were not directly measured and the study was cross-sectional, the model's wider pathways could not be tested.
Problem-focused coping was significantly associated with lower distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms only in Poland.
Emotion-focused coping was positively associated with symptoms in 11 of the 12 models; the exception was K10 in Poland.
These findings align with theoretical expectations and with studies conducted in Poland and Romania [42, 44, 47].

text.text: Because coping and symptoms were measured concurrently, the results do not establish the direction of the association.
Further comparative research should examine why problem-focused coping was associated with lower symptoms only in Poland.
The study found cross-country differences in distress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms among respondents from Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary.
Symptom levels were generally highest in Poland and lowest in Czechia, although not every pairwise country difference was statistically significant.
The findings are consistent with the possibility that prolonged warrelated stressors are relevant to mental health beyond Ukraine.
However, the cross-sectional design does not establish that the war caused the observed symptoms or country differences.
The average item-level selection rate was higher for problem-focused than for emotion-focused strategies in all four countries, although respondents reported using strategies from both categories.
Older age and higher perceived quality of life were consistently associated with lower symptom levels.
Greater social support was associated with lower K10 distress in all four countries and lower GAD-7 scores in Hungary.
For PHQ-9, social support was positively associated with scores in Slovakia and inversely associated with scores in Hungary.
Problemfocused coping was associated with lower symptoms in Poland, while emotion-focused coping was positively associated with symptoms in 11 of the 12 models; the exception was K10 in Poland.
Higher institutional trust was also associated with lower symptom scores in selected country-specific models.

Overall, the findings identify individual, social, and institutional resources as correlates of mental health during prolonged uncertainty and may inform public health monitoring and the planning of accessible psychosocial support.
This study has several limitations.
First, the data were collected through online research panels using quota sampling.
People with limited internet access or a lower likelihood of participating in online surveys may have been underrepresented; the samples should therefore not be considered nationally representative.
Second, the cross-sectional design does not allow causal conclusions or assessment of changes in mental health since the outbreak of the war.
Longitudinal studies or comparisons with suitable pre-war data would be needed to examine change over time.
Third, the study relied on self-reported measures, which may be affected by recall or reporting bias.
Finally, K10, GAD-7, and PHQ-9 scores measure reported symptoms and should not be interpreted as clinical diagnoses.
The study also did not directly measure societal resilience or public policy preparedness, which are shown as downstream domains in the conceptual model.
Consequently, it could not test all the pathways proposed in that model.

Public health authorities in countries affected by nearby armed conflict should continue to monitor mental health symptoms and ensure access to psychosocial support for groups reporting greater distress.
Responses should be adapted to national contexts and informed by ongoing assessments of population needs.
